newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik gangs believe power comes from barrel of gun.
newsitem.headline: Tajik gangs believe power comes from barrel of gun.

text.p: They fight for a dizzying array of competing warlords but ragged gunmen in the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan are united in their belief that power grows out of the barrel of a gun.
On the roads and villages, gunmen step out of the shade of a tree and into the heat to wave down cars to "check for weapons".
But these self-appointed upholders of local order want usually to levy a fee on passing traffic, much like the armed bands in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Four years of civil war in the impoverished republic of 5.7 million has made a Kalashnikov assault rifle the quickest path to riches.

The latest unrest, in which two rival warlords fought in the capital Dushanbe at the weekend while an ambitious government commander joined the fray from the south, has seen fighters of all stripes appear to stake out territory.
Their sloppy army fatigues, sunglasses and bandanas are de rigeur for the gunmen, whose swaggering gait and tough drawl reveal a widespread admiration for the films of Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Some wear white shrouds over their heads with only a slit for their eyes for added menace. Asked who they fight for, they often only reply with a gruff: "We're local".
But their thin, ill-fed bodies and battered weapons, sometimes ancient hunting rifles, mean would-be "terminators" fall way short of their muscle-bound hero.
"What a mess," said a Tajik driver under his breath at a checkpoint in the aluminium producing town of Tursunzade, about 65 km (40 miles) west of Dushanbe.

"Why can't they be properly turned out like the Russians?" he said in reference to members of a peacekeeping force deployed in Tajikistan by the Commonwealth of Independent States, whose neat posts make a stark contrast.

With state wages often little more than five dollars a month -- if they are paid -- power hungry warlords, in or outside the government, have little problem finding volunteers for private armies with the promise of plunder.

The presidential guard, allied with the armed group which won control of a contested district in Dushanbe at the weekend, wasted no time on Monday in seizing the Tursunzade aluminium smelter, one of the republic's few cash cows.
Civil war and gun law has claimed tens of thousands of lives in this mountainous Central Asian state.

Amleddin Idiyev, 14, was shopping for potatoes in a Dushanbe bazaar when fighting erupted on Saturday. Caught in the crossfire, a blast from a grenade severed an artery in his arm and lodged shrapnel in both his spindly legs.
Lying bandaged in Dushanbe's Karabolo hospital, his heart feathering under his bare chest, Idiyev shook his head violently and clicked his tongue in the negative when asked if he admired the gunmen.
"I want to be a doctor," he said resolutely.
